and many died in the press,
men, women, and children;
and others died on the roads,
and those who remained did not know where to go.
Then Nicephorus destroyed the mosque,
and threw down the two walls of the city and the courtyards.
And he remained twenty-two days in Cilicia,
and captured fifty-four fortresses,
some of them by the sword,
and some of them by surrender.
It is related
that at one of the fortresses,
whose masters had taken an oath and surrendered it,
when the Arab women were coming out,
some of the Armenians assaulted them.
A spirit of zeal seized their husbands,
and they drew swords.
Then Nicephorus the Domestic was enraged against the Arabs who drew swords,
and they killed four hundred men and a multitude of women.
And because the Fast of the Forty Days (Lent) had arrived,
Nicephorus and those with him departed for Caesarea,
intending to return again after the feast.
Now the commander of the Arabs who was in Tarsus gathered four thousand men and went out against the Romans,
and he was defeated and killed,
he and all the Arabs who were with him,
as well as the brother of Ibn al-Zayyat {OCR? / Bar Ribab}, the commander of Tarsus.
And again the Romans entered Cilicia,
and captured the fortress of Sis,
and placed guards in it and in the rest of the fortresses;
and they left and marched against Aleppo.
And Sayf al-Dawla went out and engaged the Romans,
and he was defeated.
And all the Hamdanids were killed,
while Sayf al-Dawla alone, with a few men, fled and escaped.
And the Domestic captured his palace, which was outside the wall of the city,
and took from it three hundred and ninety talents of silver,
and two thousand four hundred mules,
and countless weapons,
and he burned the palace.
And he encamped against the city,
and made a breach in its wall.
And the Romans entered,
and they made a great slaughter in it until they grew weary {OCR?}.
And they found in it one thousand two hundred Roman men who were imprisoned,
and they released them.
And they took captive more than ten thousand boys and girls,
and great plunder, as much as they were able to carry,
and the rest they burned with fire.
And they came to pits that were full of olive oil,
and filled them with water until all the oil floated and came out and poured over the ground and was ruined.
